extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers and policymakers interested in Israeli media policy and press freedom
extracted.subtask_description: Overview and descriptive summary of the laws, institutions, practices, and incidents that govern and exemplify censorship and media restrictions in Israel. Includes rules, statutory provisions, institutional powers, common practices, and notable cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and mandate of the Israeli Military Censor
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship in Israel is officially carried out by the Israeli Military Censor, a unit in the Israeli government officially tasked with carrying out preventive censorship regarding the publication of information that might affect the security of Israel. The body is headed by the Israeli Chief Censor, a military official appointed by Israel's Minister of Defense, who bestows upon the Chief Censor the authority to suppress information he deems compromising from being made public in the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of subjects the censor has targeted include Israel's nuclear weapons program and military operations outside its borders. The page provides quantitative context (e.g., averages of articles censored per year) to indicate scope and practice. The mandate is preventive: prior review and suppression of material judged to affect national security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-submission requirement for potentially controversial topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles concerning potentially controversial topics must be submitted to the Israeli Military Censor in advance; failing to do so may cause the reporter to lose their right to work as a journalist in Israel and, in the case of foreign reporters, to be barred from the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a legal/administrative obligation with enforcement consequences (loss of accreditation, barring foreigners). The text implies that the rule covers a broad set of 'potentially controversial' topics without an exhaustive public list, making prior submission a practical requirement for journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalist accreditation by the Government Press Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Every journalist working within Israel is required to be accredited by the Israeli Government Press Office. The office is allowed to deny applications based on political or security considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accreditation is a gatekeeping mechanism: denial can be on political or security grounds. The requirement functions as an administrative control over who may report from within Israel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gag orders as a tool of suppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and authorities can issue gag orders preventing Israeli media from reporting facts about particular cases (examples: Anat Kamm–Uri Blau affair, Prisoner X affair, other high-profile cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gag orders can be long-lasting and may be partially lifted to allow quoting foreign press reports but not original reporting. Social media and foreign outlets sometimes bypass local gag orders, and such orders attract criticism and legal challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Al Jazeera law: power to close foreign news networks and seize equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Al Jazeera law' gives the Israeli government the power to close foreign news networks operating in the country and confiscate their equipment if they are deemed to be threats to national security. The law can be applied for an initial 45-day period but can be renewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law was passed (71 to 10 vote) and was planned to be used against Al Jazeera; instances described include the seizure of Associated Press equipment alleged to be providing information to Al Jazeera. The entry shows how statutory measures can be used to target specific foreign broadcasters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational-security censorship rules (what may not be reported)
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship rules largely concern military issues such as not reporting if a missile hit or missed its target, troop movements, etc.; the censor is also empowered to control information about the oil industry and water supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During conflicts the censor prohibits publication of details like Iranian missile impacts, defensive interceptor locations, and certain images/footage deemed operationally sensitive. Written authorization is required for broadcasts originating from a 'war zone or missile strike site' and foreign journalists were noted as prohibited from filming locations affected by strikes in some conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties and enforcement (criminal prosecution, closure of newspapers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists who bypass the military censor or publish items that were censored may be subject to criminal prosecution and jail time; the censor also has the authority to close newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While severe measures exist, the page notes they have been rarely used historically. Notable exceptions (e.g., closure tied to Kav 300 affair) are described; the text documents both the legal powers and their occasional exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal defamation and insulting public officials as media constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to the possibility of civil defamation suits, journalists can also be charged with criminal defamation and 'insulting a public official'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters Without Borders notes these criminal risks, and the page highlights that confidentiality of sources is not protected by statutory law, increasing legal vulnerability for journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory prohibitions on hate speech and support for terrorist organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Israeli law outlaws hate speech and 'expressing support for illegal or terrorist organizations'. Section 173 makes it a crime to publish any 'publication that is liable to crudely offend the religious faith or sentiment of others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutory provisions set content-based limits on publication and have been applied alongside military/security censorship and other media regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions affecting Palestinian press and journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Israeli forces have subjected Palestinian journalists to arrest, interrogation, and administrative detention, often without clear grounds; several Palestinian media outlets have been closed for allegedly inciting violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters Without Borders and other organizations have raised concerns about harassment, smear campaigns, closures, and travel bans that prevent Palestinian journalists from leaving the West Bank and Gaza. The page cites specific instances and international condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel bans and movement restrictions on journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Travel bans that prevent dozens of Palestinian journalists from leaving the West Bank and Gaza Strip; in many cases these bans have remained in place for years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named organizations (RSF, Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor) have called for ending such bans. The restriction functions as an indirect censorship/limitation on reporting opportunities and international engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of military orders to close civil society organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Military orders have been used to impose the closure of offices of Palestinian human rights groups after accusing them of operating as fronts for terrorist organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes international condemnation (UN and others) of such closures; the practice illustrates how security classifications can be applied to civil society and media-adjacent organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Film and cultural censorship criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Film censorship and media regulation have been applied for reasons including harm to diplomatic relations, excessive cruelty, libel, the possibility of offending the public, or 'hurting the feelings of believers' (examples: bans on specific films cited year-by-year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some bans were later overturned by the Supreme Court (e.g., The Last Temptation of Christ, Jenin, Jenin). Historical examples show both the applied criteria and judicial checks on cultural censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial oversight and limits on military censorship (Editors' Committee agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 1996 agreement allowed military censorship only of articles clearly harmful to national security and allowed the Supreme Court to override military decisions; the Editors' Committee resumed operation under this framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indicates an institutional and legal check on the censor's power, illustrating that censorship practice has been shaped by agreements and court interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common circumvention strategy: leaking to foreign media
rubrics_metrics.description: A commonly used way for Israeli media to circumvent censorship rules is to leak items to foreign news sources, which by virtue of being located outside of Israel are not subject to Israeli censorship. Once published, the Israeli media can simply quote the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page presents this as a practical workaround used by local outlets and bloggers; it also highlights the role of foreign publications in exposing locally suppressed stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of gag orders and censorship during specific conflicts (war-time intensification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Military censorship has peaked during periods of conflict (e.g., Twelve-Day War, 2026 Iran War), with restrictions on publication of strikes, details of missile impacts, and other operationally sensitive material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents intensified enforcement (e.g., prohibiting publication about soldier disappearances, banning certain on-the-ground reporting) and notes the practical effect: limited real-time reporting and restrictions on visual material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative indicators of censorship activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistics reported for military censor activity: e.g., 'On average, 2,240 press articles in Israel are censored by the Israeli Military Censor each year, approximately 240 of which in full, and around 2,000 partially.' Other figures given for later years (e.g., 2017, 2018, 2024, 2025) enumerate outright bans and redactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statistics are used in the article to indicate scale and trends of censorship (including reported spikes in particular years). They provide an empirical metric to evaluate the intensity of censorship over time.
